item.title: End-to-End Quantum Algorithm for Differential Equations: Application to Simulating a Biomolecular System
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article marks a concrete step toward usable quantum differential‑equation solvers by delivering an end‑to‑end pipeline that starts from classical data and returns classical observables for the linearized Poisson‑Boltzmann equation, a workhorse in biomolecular modeling. By introducing a new grid representation for variable‑coefficient PDEs and leveraging wavelet preconditioning, the authors achieve polylogarithmic gate complexity in both problem size and target precision—eliminating the condition‑number bottleneck that has hampered earlier proposals. If fault‑tolerant hardware catches up, such an approach could give quantum computers a practical edge in high‑resolution electrostatic simulations for drug discovery and protein engineering.

Quantum algorithms for differential equations have the potential for substantial algorithmic speedups over classical methods. However, they rely on certain assumptions and abstract oracle specifications that leave their practical feasibility and computational advantages for realistic applications unclear. Here we formalize the concept of an end-to-end quantum algorithm for differential equations as one that accepts classical inputs and returns classical outputs, and provide implementations for algorithmic primitives in constructing such algorithms. We present a tailored end-to-end quantum algorithm for the linearized Poisson-Boltzmann (LPB) equation, a partial differential equation (PDE) with variable coefficients widely used in simulating a biomolecular system. We explicitly implement all aspects of the algorithm, from preparing an initial state to generating a quantum solution and estimating properties of the system. In particular, we develop a new discrete representation for variable-coefficient PDEs on a grid that enables efficient implementation of the operator oracle, and build on a recent technique based on optimal wavelet preconditioning to generate a quantum solution with a cost independent of the condition number of the discretized operator. We show the algorithm can be implemented by quantum circuits of size polylogarithmic in both the number of grid points $N_g$ and the inverse of the desired accuracy $\varepsilon$, with an overall gate cost polylogarithmic in $N_g$ and quasilinear in $1/\varepsilon$. We also show the classical preprocessing to construct the circuits has polylogarithmic cost in $N_g$ and $1/\varepsilon$. Our work provides a concrete end-to-end quantum algorithm for a PDE of practical value, demonstrates an exponential improvement in scaling with $N_g$ over classical methods, and provides a foundation for assessing its potential quantum advantage in practice.

item.title: Authenticating quantum key distribution through random position checks
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article shows that a party’s geographic position can serve as the authentication credential in BB84‑based quantum key distribution, dramatically cutting the overhead by interleaving lightweight quantum‑position‑verification rounds instead of running a full QPV protocol for every bit. By marrying QKD with location‑based security, it tackles one of the most practical hurdles—efficient, trustworthy authentication—and dovetails with recent pushes toward measurement‑device‑independent and satellite‑based QKD where spatial information is already a key resource. The authors’ initial security analysis covers only a restricted class of attacks, so broader composable proofs will be needed before deployment, but the approach points to a promising route for scaling authenticated quantum communications.

Quantum key distribution (QKD) requires some form of authentication in order for the parties to be sure they are not unknowingly generating a key with an adversary pretending to be one of the honest parties. In this work, we propose a protocol in which the position of one of the parties is used as the authentication credential for key distribution. Our protocol essentially consists of a BB84 QKD protocol with quantum position verification (QPV) rounds randomly interleaved in. The approach is efficient compared with previous approaches, which required running an entire QPV protocol for every bit requiring authentication. We undertake an initial security analysis of the protocol for a restricted set of attacks.

item.title: On the design of sequential quantum repeaters with error detection
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article shows that modest quantum error‑detecting codes—especially two‑qubit repetition or parity encodings—can already give a measurable boost to long‑distance, trust‑free QKD when deployed in sequential repeater chains, narrowing the gap between today’s noisy hardware and fully fault‑tolerant networks. By rigorously comparing entanglement‑generation architectures and quantifying how incremental improvements in memory lifetimes or photon‑collection efficiencies translate into higher secret‑key rates, the work connects directly to ongoing experimental efforts on fiber‑based repeaters and satellite links. The findings suggest that near‑term quantum‑communication deployments may not need heavyweight error correction, but rather a carefully chosen lightweight code plus targeted hardware upgrades, offering a realistic pathway toward scalable quantum networks.

Long-distance, trust-free quantum communications rely on the development of scalable quantum repeater schemes. Sequential entanglement generation with error detection is a promising approach that combines manageable implementation requirements with a hop-by-hop architecture compatible with existing classical infrastructure. In this paper, we investigate key design choices for such schemes over a repeater chain using quantum key distribution as a benchmark. We find that simple quantum error-detecting codes, such as repetition codes or quantum parity codes, perform well under near-term hardware assumptions and outperform strategies without any encoding. In particular, we show that two-qubit repetition codes may well be all that we need to implement in many practical scenarios. We also examine different architectures for the generation of initial entanglement and assess their merits. Additionally, we show that moderate improvements in some hardware components can partially mitigate the slow technological progress of others.

item.title: Optimal Error corrected Hamiltonian estimation with nuisance parameters
item.description:
Curator's Take: This work overturns a long‑standing assumption that nuisance parameters must be locally suppressed in error‑corrected quantum sensors, showing instead that only Markovian noise needs active correction while coherent control can simply separate unwanted drifts from the signal over the full interrogation time. By proving a necessary and sufficient condition for Heisenberg‑limited precision under realistic Hamiltonian dynamics, the authors expand the parameter regimes where quadratic scaling is achievable—an advance that could immediately inform the design of next‑generation atomic clocks, magnetometers, and distributed sensor networks. The result also clarifies why recent experiments using dynamical decoupling or tailored pulse sequences have succeeded despite residual systematic drifts, pointing to a broader, more flexible blueprint for robust quantum metrology.

Realistic quantum sensing is often affected by both noise and unknown nuisance parameters. Under Markovian dynamics, existing error correction approaches have often sought to suppress nuisance responses alongside environmental noise. Here we show that this local suppression of nuisance parameters is unnecessary and can be overly restrictive: nuisance parameters and Markovian noise impose fundamentally different constraints and require distinct treatments. We establish a general framework for quantum sensing with parameters encoded in a general time dependent Hamiltonian, in the presence of both nuisance parameters and Markovian noise. We derive a necessary and sufficient condition for Heisenberg scaling, determine the exact optimal precision, and construct protocols that attain it. Our results show that to achieve Heisenberg scaling Markovian noise must be suppressed locally by quantum error correction, whereas nuisance parameters need not, and in general should not, be eliminated locally. Instead, optimally designed coherent control can separate their accumulated effects from the target signal over the full sensing evolution. Consequently, Heisenberg scaling can remain attainable even when the target signal is instantaneously aligned with nuisance parameter directions, in sharp contrast to alignment with Markovian noise. This distinction substantially enlarges the regime in which Heisenberg scaling is attainable and provides a general principle for designing robust quantum sensors.

item.title: Scaling classical hardware for accurate real-time quantum error correction
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article shows that the classical side of fault‑tolerant quantum computing can finally keep pace with today’s fast superconducting processors by delivering a decoder that is both sub‑microsecond and dramatically more accurate than existing real‑time solutions. By co‑designing a neural network to run on an FPGA in integer arithmetic, the Rapids decoder cuts logical error rates by two orders of magnitude while preserving the low latency required for surface‑code cycles, directly reducing the qubit overhead that has limited scalable experiments. The demonstrated scalability across multiple FPGAs and the path toward ASIC implementation signal that classical hardware will become a first‑class resource in future quantum architectures, easing one of the biggest bottlenecks on the road to practical error correction.

Fault-tolerant quantum computation requires a classical decoder fast enough to process syndrome measurements at the rate at which they are generated, and to return its decisions with low latency. This is most demanding for superconducting processors, whose fast syndrome cycles force a trade-off between decoding speed and accuracy. Decoders fast enough to keep up sacrifice accuracy, which must be compensated for with larger codes and thus additional physical qubits. Here we introduce Rapids, a streaming neural decoder that is both fast and accurate. We achieve this by co-designing the decoder with a field-programmable gate array (FPGA): the network is built from operations that map cheaply onto the device and trained in its integer arithmetic. For the distance-19 surface code, Rapids decodes each round of syndromes in under a microsecond on a single FPGA, fast enough for superconducting processors, and returns its decisions with the low latency that fault-tolerant algorithms require. Its logical error rate is 240 times lower than that of existing real-time hardware decoders. The same design extends to the color code and the [[144,12,12]] bivariate-bicycle code, on which our decoder is 16 times more accurate than the real-time Relay decoder. We further show that the decoder scales: spread over several FPGAs or hardened into custom silicon, it becomes faster, more accurate, or able to decode larger codes. Classical hardware thus becomes a further resource, alongside qubits, that can be scaled to improve fault-tolerant quantum computers.

item.title: When lies look like noise: certifying untrusted entanglement swapping
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article tackles a subtle but critical security gap in entanglement‑swapping repeaters by showing that dishonest nodes can hide misreported measurement outcomes behind ordinary readout noise, making standard verification ineffective. By introducing a cut‑and‑choose certification scheme that tests only a random subset while preserving the remaining pairs for use, it offers a realistic quality‑of‑service guarantee compatible with emerging quantum‑network protocols. The analysis also highlights today’s memory bottleneck—certifying even a modest 1 % misreport rate on a million links would require storing up to a million entangled pairs—underscoring the need for scalable quantum memories before such safeguards can be deployed at scale.

Entanglement swapping lets quantum repeaters distribute entanglement over long distances, a prerequisite for the quantum internet. We study its security in a noisy network whose intermediate nodes perform the quantum operations faithfully but may misreport the classical outcome that end users rely on. We show that the ideal functionality of entanglement swapping cannot be realised, because it gives the adversary no influence over the delivered state, whereas a node that relabels its report does have such influence. Including honest noise in the ideal setting does not help unless it also concedes a bounded fraction of misreported pairs. We therefore propose a cut-and-choose protocol that tests a random subset of pairs to certify the rest. Since no test can distinguish a misreport from readout noise, the protocol certifies the error above a pre-agreed minimum noise level, which is the misreport rate under our threat model. This yields a quality-of-service guarantee, in which a failure witnesses that the node did not deliver as agreed. Unlike verification schemes that consume the state they certify, the untested pairs remain available for use, with a finite-size guarantee. Certifying a 1% misreport rate on 10^6 pairs costs 10^4 to 1.7x10^5 test pairs, for minimum noise levels ranging from 0 to 5%. The main cost is memory, since 1% requires holding 10^5 to 10^6 pairs at once, far beyond the capacity of today's quantum memories. Verifying and releasing in blocks ties the memory to the block size at the cost of a weaker rate: a (10^4)-qubit memory certifies 14% on 4.7x10^5 delivered pairs.

item.title: Tunable Ground-State Entanglement in Fully Connected Quantum Systems: From Logarithmic to Volume-Law Scaling
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article shows that by simply tweaking the strength‑scaling exponent of all‑to‑all couplings, one can continuously dial a system’s ground‑state entanglement from the familiar logarithmic bound up to a full volume law, something previously thought impossible for gapped, nondegenerate states. The result bridges theoretical work on Kac‑normalized models with the practical reality of hardware platforms such as trapped‑ion and superconducting arrays that naturally exhibit long‑range interactions, offering a new knob to engineer entanglement complexity without changing the underlying connectivity. It also warns that even modest departures from the canonical normalization can erase universal entanglement limits, a consideration that will matter for designing scalable quantum simulators and error‑corrected architectures.

Entanglement scaling is a central probe of the complexity of quantum many-body ground states, yet once geometric locality is absent, it can depend sensitively on the structure and normalization of interactions. For fully connected Hamiltonians with the natural Kac normalization, nondegenerate gapped ground states are known to obey a logarithmic entanglement bound. Here we ask how the ground-state entanglement changes when this interaction normalization is continuously relaxed away from the Kac scale. We answer this question by constructing an explicit all-to-all bipartite Hamiltonian of $n$ qubits with Fourier pairing amplitudes and pairwise interaction strength proportional to $n^{-κ}$. For sufficiently small fixed coupling, we prove that every pure ground state has entanglement entropy $Θ(n^{2-2κ} \log n)$ for $1/2<κ\leq1$ and $Θ(n)$ at $κ=1/2$. We further show that the ground state is unique and separated from the rest of the spectrum by a system-size-independent gap for $3/4 \leq κ\leq 1$, while weak-coupling analysis and numerical calculations suggest that the gap remains open also for $1/2 \leq κ< 3/4$. Thus, varying only the interaction normalization yields a controlled hierarchy from logarithmic scaling at the natural Kac normalization $κ=1$ to increasingly strong subextensive entanglement and ultimately to a volume law, showing that even an arbitrarily weak relaxation of this normalization precludes a universal logarithmic entanglement bound.

item.title: Non-Binary Detector Error Models
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article shows that the long‑standing simplification of circuit‑level noise into binary detector error models can be lifted without sacrificing decoding simplicity, by representing each fault location with a single non‑binary random variable that captures the full Pauli alphabet. The resulting non‑binary DEMs exactly describe any Clifford‑based syndrome extraction circuit, produce Tanner graphs with dramatically fewer edges and improve decoder performance on surface, color and bicycle codes—an advance that directly addresses the scalability bottlenecks highlighted in recent Stim and fault‑tolerant QEC studies. By keeping belief‑propagation messages scalar, the approach promises more hardware‑friendly decoders while preserving—or even enhancing—the error‑suppression needed for practical quantum computers.

A key challenge in fault-tolerant quantum error correction (QEC) is that the syndrome extraction circuits are themselves faulty. Such circuit-level noise is commonly described by a detector error model (DEM). In Stim and in almost all related works, DEMs are binary: every non-binary circuit error (e.g., CNOT gate), is decomposed into independent binary error mechanisms. In this work, we introduce non-binary DEMs, in which each fault location of the syndrome extraction circuit is modeled by one random variable over its original alphabet, e.g., the 16 two-qubit Pauli errors after a CNOT gate. We also propose a split-merge-regroup transformation that builds a compact non-binary DEM from any Clifford circuit by merging the error components that flip the same detectors and observables. Non-binary DEMs represent any Pauli channel exactly, whereas binary DEMs are exact only for channels that factorize into independent binary parts. When the channels factorize, we prove that binary and non-binary DEMs are equivalent under degenerate quantum maximum-a-posteriori (MAP) decoding, but not under quantum MAP decoding. Although the variables are non-binary, belief propagation (BP) still exchanges a single scalar message per edge. Our numerical results with surface, color and bivariate bicycle codes show that non-binary DEMs have two main advantages. First, their Tanner graphs have four to five times fewer edges, which is advantageous for hardware implementations. Second, their performance under BP, with and without OSD post-processing, is better than that of their binary counterparts, and BP with OSD runs up to $9.4\times$ faster in a CPU.

item.title: Quantum Zeno Effect with a Superposed Measurement Schedule in Relational Time
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article demonstrates a concrete way to put the timing of measurements themselves into a quantum superposition, turning the classic Quantum Zeno effect into a probe of relational time that can be realized on today’s superconducting‑qubit platforms. By showing that interference between two distinct measurement schedules depends only on their relative offset—and that a single schedule can even reverse the usual Zeno freezing— the work opens a new experimental handle for testing foundational ideas while also suggesting novel sensing schemes where timing coherence boosts resolution. The authors back up the proposal with realistic gate counts and error budgets, making it a timely bridge between abstract Page‑Wootters concepts and near‑term hardware demonstrations.

Motivated by the Page-Wootters construction in which time is a quantum clock reading and the global system state is stationary, we propose a quantum circuit that explores the observable consequences of treating measurement timing as a quantum degree of freedom. We place two Zeno measurement schedules of a driven qubit in a coherent superposition using a schedule qubit. We show that, for a fixed drive strength, the interference visibility between the two schedules depends only on the time offset between them, not on the number of intermediate measurements taken. Then we show that, for one schedule-readout outcome, the Zeno trend reverses, predicting a result that complements the standard Zeno probability. We propose a circuit implementation with physical memory qubits and show that measuring the memory register's joint $X$-basis parity distinguishes a coherent schedule from a classical or dephased one. We give the gate count and an error budget for a superconducting-qubit implementation. The Page-Wootters picture motivates this protocol and provides an equivalent stationary representation, although the predictions follow from the standard circuit description without requiring a relational-time interpretation. This is consistent with the Page-Wootters framework recovering standard quantum dynamics through correlations between a clock and the rest of the system.

item.title: Entanglement, records, and quantum recovery in qubit chains
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article demonstrates for the first time how a simple, exactly solvable qubit chain can separate the spread of entanglement from the emergence of locally readable information, revealing that weak interactions let quantum correlations outrun any measurable record on a neighboring site. By showing that off‑diagonal elements of a reduced density matrix serve as the leading “record” detectable with a single Pauli measurement—and by quantifying optimal recovery fidelities when only a fragment of the environment is accessible—the work bridges fundamental studies of decoherence with practical concerns in quantum error correction and sensor design. The finding that intra‑environment interactions can reshuffle readable records without altering the system’s reduced state suggests new strategies for engineering protective environments that preserve recoverable information while minimizing disturbance to the processor itself.

We investigate entanglement, readable records and quantum recovery using an exactly solvable chain of sequentially interacting qubits. For weak interactions, entanglement reaches a later environment site before that site carries an equally strong local record. The leading local record is encoded in an off-diagonal element of the reduced density matrix and can be detected by a Pauli measurement, while a population measurement gives a higher-order signal. We further characterize the accessibility of the relative phase through joint transverse correlations and derive the optimal fidelity for recovering an unknown quantum state from the system and an accessible environment fragment. We show that interactions acting only within the environment can redistribute readable records and change the region required for quantum recovery without affecting the reduced state of the system.

item.title: Quantum Autoencoder on Real Hardware for New Physics Searches at Muon Colliders
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article marks one of the first demonstrations that a quantum autoencoder can be run on real‑world hardware to tackle a high‑energy physics problem, showing that a six‑qubit circuit on the Tianyan176 processor already distinguishes Standard Model tri‑photon events from anomalous quartic gauge‑coupling signatures. By delivering reconstruction‑loss based discrimination comparable to classical analyses, it highlights how near‑term quantum machine‑learning tools could become part of the data‑analysis pipeline for future muon colliders, where massive event rates will demand ultra‑efficient pattern recognition. The work also underscores current limitations—noise and qubit count still constrain scalability—but sets a clear benchmark for how quantum‑enhanced searches for new physics might evolve as hardware improves.

We apply a quantum autoencoder to search for new physics (NP) in the tri-photon process $μ^+μ^-\toγγγ$ at muon colliders. Using a six-qubit circuit on the Tianyan176 quantum computer, we measure the reconstruction losses for Standard Model (SM) events and anomalous quartic gauge couplings (aQGCs) events. The results demonstrate that the hardware-implemented quantum autoencoder effectively discriminates NP signals from the SM background. Concurrently, we derive the expected constraints on the aQGCs coefficients and compare them with those obtained from conventional methods.

item.title: Quantifying the irrealism required by quantum random access codes
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article provides the first quantitative link between a fundamental notion of “irrealism” – how far measurement outcomes deviate from having pre‑existing values – and the performance of quantum random access codes, a benchmark task for communication‑limited quantum processors. By mapping out exact irrealism frontiers for both prepare‑and‑measure and entanglement‑assisted schemes, it shows that modest amounts of nonclassical disturbance are sufficient to surpass classical success rates, while higher advantages demand genuine realism‑based nonlocality in the shared resource. The results give experimentalists a concrete metric for assessing how much coherence or entanglement their hardware must retain to achieve a target QRAC advantage, and they clarify why simply using mutually unbiased bases is not always the most resource‑efficient strategy.

How far must decoding observables be from having elements of reality to achieve a given quantum advantage in a communication task? We answer this question for quantum random access codes. Here, an observable has an element of reality when its unrevealed measurement leaves the preparation undisturbed; its irrealism is the relative entropy to the closest such preparation. Because it comprises local coherence and the correlations destroyed by the unrevealed measurement, irrealism applies to prepare-and-measure (PM) and entanglement-assisted (EA) codes alike. For PM codes decoded in mutually unbiased bases, we obtain the irrealism frontier, the least total irrealism compatible with each success probability, exactly in every dimension; an excess-irrealism identity shows that Gibbs states of the decoding operator attain it uniquely. For PM codes minimized also over the decoders, the required irrealism vanishes up to the classical value and is positive beyond it; for qubits, mutually unbiased decoders are not the cheapest below a success probability of 0.833. For EA codes with a qubit receiver, trusted decoders, and parity-dependent sender settings, the frontier exceeds the PM one by the realism-based nonlocality of the contexts used by an optimal code, and with rank-one projective sender measurements a success probability above 0.815 certifies a minimum realism-based nonlocality of the shared state.

item.title: Stitching Quantum Codes into Quilts: Universal Logic with no Ancillary Qubits
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article shows how logical Pauli‑product measurements can be carried out across multiple code blocks without adding any extra data qubits, a step that could dramatically cut the overhead of fault‑tolerant architectures beyond the surface code. By framing the measurement as a “code quilt” built from subsystem‑code gauge generators, the authors demonstrate concrete circuits that keep physical qubit degree low and preserve code‑capacity distance in extensive simulations on bicycle and surface codes. While the first variant is not provably fault tolerant at asymptotic distances and the second lacks a general proof, the empirical results suggest a practical pathway toward more resource‑efficient error correction and multi‑code logical operations.

Proposals abound for performing fault-tolerant logical Pauli-product measurements between quantum codes beyond the surface code. We introduce a new construction, the code quilt, whereby a target joint logical operator of two or more codeblocks is directly measured without the use of an ancillary system. We construct explicit circuits to perform a logical measurement using the quilt construction, which also require no physical qubits beyond the ancillas already in place to perform idle syndrome extraction on the codeblocks in question. We give a detailed structural analysis of the construction, which is based on a subsystem code, and provide several sets of sufficient conditions under which the relevant code-capacity distance is preserved. We give two variants of the protocol. The first, where the gauge generators of the subsystem code are measured directly, is provably not fault tolerant in the large-distance limit but admits a particularly practical circuit implementation in which the physical qubit degree increases by at most two. The second has more favourable asymptotic properties, although we do not prove its fault tolerance in the general case. We then perform an extensive empirical analysis of the technique, in particular of the first variant, as applied to bivariate bicycle and surface codes, finding code-capacity-distance preserving quilts for measuring 25,000 randomly selected logical operators. We optimise to find sparse and decongested detector bases for each and, for a randomly selected subset, find circuits that we estimate to be distance preserving. Finally, we perform decoding experiments on a subset of these circuits and find that their logical error probability is comparable to that of idle memory for operations involving the 144-qubit bivariate bicycle code and distance-12 rotated surface code at physical error rates between $1.5\times 10^{-3}$ and $3\times 10^{-3}$.

item.title: All Non-Contextual Pauli Hamiltonians are Free-Fermion in Disguise
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article proves that any non‑contextual Pauli Hamiltonian is secretly a free‑fermion model, establishing a concrete bridge between contextual subspace decompositions and the well‑understood physics of free fermions. By formalising the proof in Lean and delivering a heuristic line‑graph algorithm to pull out free‑fermion fragments from molecular Hamiltonians, it gives practitioners a new, classically tractable way to carve up problems before handing them to a quantum processor. The result could shrink the quantum workload for chemistry simulations by allowing larger portions of the Hamiltonian to be solved exactly on classical hardware, although its effectiveness will depend on how often realistic molecules admit the required graph structure.

Decomposing Hamiltonians into classically tractable fragments is central to quantum simulation. One such way of doing so is the contextual subspace decomposition, which expresses the Hamiltonian with respect to non-contextual sets of Paulis. The conditions for contextuality rely on the anticommutation and commutation of Pauli operators; it is therefore natural to make an explicit connection between non-contextuality and fermionic physics. Theoretical work is centered around two theorems: in the first, we consider non-contextual Pauli Hamiltonians and show that they are free-fermion-disguised. In the second we write these Pauli non-contextual Hamiltonians in terms of Majorana and Dirac fermionic operators, showing that they carry a Jordan--Wigner-like fermion-to-qubit encoding. These two central theorems are formalized in the proof assistant language Lean. We use this to describe the space of fermionic non-contextual Hamiltonians, and highlight their relation to the more general class of free-fermion-disguised Hamiltonians. We further develop a heuristic algorithm to find line-graph based free-fermion fragments and their connected components of molecular Hamiltonians. We benchmark our algorithms against non-contextual searches for encoded molecular Hamiltonians and find comparable performance in identifying free-fermion solvable components. Our work has implications for what fragments to consider as useful for quantum simulation.

item.title: Efficient calculation of the full Laguerre-Gaussian spectrum of entangled biphotons
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article delivers a compact analytical tool that replaces the brute‑force multidimensional integrals normally required to predict the full Laguerre‑Gaussian spectrum of SPDC biphotons, making it practical to explore very high radial and OAM orders without numerical instability. By expressing the source geometry in just a few dimensionless parameters, researchers can now rapidly optimize pump and crystal settings to approach maximal high‑dimensional entanglement—a key step for scaling orbital‑angular‑momentum based quantum communication and photonic processors. The work builds on recent efforts to harness OAM for large Hilbert spaces but overcomes the longstanding bottleneck of computational cost, although experimental validation will still be needed to confirm how closely real devices follow the idealized phase‑matching model.

The spatial biphoton state generated by spontaneous parametric down-conversion (SPDC) enables applications in high-dimensional quantum information processing and is often described in Laguerre-Gaussian (LG) modes. However, calculating the full LG spectrum for arbitrary radial and orbital angular momentum (OAM) indices requires computationally demanding multidimensional integrations. We present a generating-function approach that analytically performs the four-dimensional transverse spatial integral without approximating the phase-matching function. The source geometry can be completely described by a few dimensionless parameters, which reduce to two parameters for wave-vector-degenerate photons with equal waists. Our derived expressions for the full LG spectrum allow for computationally efficient and numerically stable evaluation at high mode orders, addressing a crucial obstacle in previous works. To illustrate our approach, we compare OAM spectra obtained by projection onto the lowest radial order and by radially insensitive detection, and investigate how high-dimensional maximal entanglement can be approached by tuning source parameters. Our results provide a new analytical tool for efficiently characterizing and engineering high-dimensional spatial entanglement in SPDC.

item.title: CAVQS: Context-Aware Variational Quantum Circuit Synthesis via Unitary Redistribution and Dynamic Reconstruction
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article introduces CAVQS, a context‑aware variational circuit synthesiser that reshapes overlapping blocks with QR‑based unitary redistribution and exploits pre‑measurement feed‑forward to prune unnecessary CNOTs. By achieving up to roughly 70 % fewer two‑qubit gates than leading tools such as QFAST, SQUANDER and Fast‑USYN, it directly tackles the dominant error source on today’s NISQ processors and could lower compilation overhead for near‑term algorithms. The work builds on recent trends of hybrid synthesis that blend unitary optimisation with measurement‑driven shortcuts, showing how cross‑block awareness can unlock savings that block‑wise methods miss. While the benchmarks are limited to 4–6 qubits, the methodology scales conceptually and points toward more hardware‑friendly compilation pipelines as devices grow larger.

Variational quantum circuit synthesis jointly searches circuit structure and continuous parameters to reduce costly two-qubit gates, but block-based workflows typically instantiate blocks independently, limiting simplification across block boundaries. Moreover, fully unitary synthesis does not exploit opportunities created by permitted output measurements and classical feedforward. We present CAVQS, a context-aware variational synthesis framework that combines unitary redistribution and dynamic reconstruction. First, CAVQS uses QR decomposition to transfer unitary factors between overlapping blocks, preserving the overall transformation while reshaping local synthesis targets to enable cross-block reductions. Second, for blocks that precede permitted terminal measurements, CAVQS constructs ancilla-free dynamic implementations with a CNOT-budgeted pre-measurement search and analytic branch-unitary construction, thereby minimizing expected CNOT cost. Across random-circuit targets, CAVQS reduces mean two-qubit gate counts by 28.79%-42.52%, 2.05%-52.62%, and 30.51%-74.64% relative to QFAST, SQUANDER, and Fast-USYN, respectively, on common successful instances. On 4--6-qubit quantum algorithm benchmarks, the corresponding reductions are 27.27%-36.77%, 20.65%-69.10%, and 36.31%-71.88%, respectively.

item.title: To predict or to persist: how decoherence shapes learning in a spin-qubit quantum reservoir
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article demonstrates that modest dephasing in a six‑qubit spin‑chain reservoir can actually improve prediction accuracy for certain nonlinear time‑series tasks, highlighting decoherence as a potential resource rather than merely a nuisance. By systematically comparing single‑ and two‑qubit readouts across a range of T₂ values, the authors connect their findings to the broader push toward hardware‑aware quantum machine‑learning algorithms that exploit NISQ‑level noise. The work also cautions that the benefit is task‑dependent—chaotic forecasting still suffers under short coherence times—so designers of quantum reservoirs must tailor both hardware and readout strategies to the specific application.

In this work we investigate how dephasing and the choice of measured observables affect learning in a simulated six-qubit spin chain with Markovian dissipation and exact expectation-value readout. For externally driven nonlinear autoregressive moving-average signals, combining single- and two-qubit observables gives better predictions than a population-only readout at comparable polynomial feature counts. Most of the configurations we tested become more accurate than a reference with relaxation and dephasing disabled, most strongly at $T_2=1\,μ$s, where total memory capacity drops, and still at $T_2=5$-$10\,μ$s, where memory is only redistributed across delays. For autonomous generation, we train the readout with scheduled sampling and iterative dataset aggregation to expose it to states reached under its own feedback. We do not find a clear systematic dependence of limit-cycle persistence on coherence across the reservoir ensemble. For chaotic forecasting, in contrast, prediction horizons at $T_2=1\,μ$s shorten in all 10 reservoir realizations relative to that reference. For the noise-driven strange non-chaotic attractor, the model produces a smooth, approximately closed orbit, and neither captures the target's scatter nor follows its trajectory pointwise. We conclude that, within this simulated reservoir, the impact of coherence depends strongly on the task.

item.title: Ellis: Extremely Fast Quantum Circuit Simulation under Qubit Loss and Leakage
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article introduces Ellis, a simulator that can model Clifford‑type fault‑tolerant circuits even when qubits are lost or leak, something traditional Pauli‑frame methods could not handle because the circuit varies shot‑by‑shot. By identifying “frame‑CSS” circuits that retain a common reference despite loss, the authors achieve near‑linear‑time certification and a staggering 952 k shots per second on a single core—orders of magnitude faster than existing tools such as Clifft or PPVM. The breakthrough opens the door to realistic large‑scale testing of error‑corrected quantum algorithms under hardware‑relevant loss and leakage, though its applicability is currently limited to circuits that fit the frame‑CSS structure.

Qubit loss and leakage are persistent errors: while a qubit remains lost or leaked, every operation acting on it is dropped. Consequently, the Clifford circuit executed differs from shot to shot. This variation breaks Pauli-frame simulation, which constructs each shot by XORing sampled Pauli flips onto a single \emph{common reference} measurement record. By rethinking the roles of tableau simulation and Pauli-frame simulation, we show that many key fault-tolerant primitives nevertheless retain a common reference under loss. These include CSS code memory, lattice surgery, and transversal CNOT. Such circuits can therefore be simulated exactly under Pauli noise and loss by a Pauli frame with per-shot masks for the dropped operations. We define \emph{frame-CSS} circuits as those that are CSS up to local single-qubit basis changes, given a loss model that specifies where qubits can be lost and reloaded. We prove that every frame-CSS circuit has a common reference, and we give a practically near-linear-time procedure that certifies whether a circuit is frame-CSS. We implement the certifier and a high-performance simulator in the open-source package \href{https://github.com/isaachyw/ELLIS}{\textsc{Ellis}} (Efficient Loss and Leakage Invariant-reference Simulation). On the gross code under qubit loss and Pauli errors, \ellis{} samples 952{,}000 shots per second on a single CPU core, at least $1000\times$ faster than Clifft~\cite{chase2026} and PPVM~\cite{luo2026ppvm}.

This can provide an additional tool for monitoring against possible eavesdropping attempts that affect the phase randomization.

item.title: The classical complexity of quantum state transmission
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article quantifies exactly how costly it is to replace genuine quantum channels with purely classical communication, showing that the required resources explode exponentially with system size and only improve polynomially as noise is reduced. By proving an equivalence between the “classical complexity” of state transmission and the cost of reproducing quantum correlations, the work provides a rigorous benchmark for any claimed quantum‑communication advantage and dovetails with recent efforts to certify quantum internet hardware. The authors also deliver scalable semidefinite‑programming tools that let experimentalists certify when their preparation devices are truly beyond classical simulation, turning an abstract complexity measure into a practical diagnostic.

Quantum communication provides a natural means to transmit quantum information, but how difficult is it to make such a transmission using only classical communication resources? We address this question by introducing classical communication models for quantum preparations and defining their minimum cost as the classical complexity. We prove that this complexity equals the amount of classical communication required to simulate quantum correlations in prepare-and-broadcast experiments, thus establishing a resource equivalence between quantum state transmission and quantum correlations. This calls for a general characterisation of the classical complexity of the noisy quantum state space, which we show grows exponentially with the quantum dimension and as a power-law in the inverse noise. It reveals the rapidly scaling fundamental cost of classical simulation. Moreover, we develop a toolbox of methods to certify classical complexity in quantum preparation devices, including an exact semidefinite-programming characterisation, analytical witnesses for symmetric preparations and convex programming scalable up to hundreds and sometimes thousands of qubit states. Our results establish classical complexity as a fundamental measure of quantum communication advantage, revealing the intrinsic cost of classically simulating quantum theory and providing practical tools for its certification.

item.description:

By quantifying the channel with realistic signal counts, the authors demonstrate up to a 6 dB advantage over single‑mode CV‑QKD and a 3 dB gain versus simple multiplexing—an improvement that could make space‑based QKD links far more efficient. Multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) techniques, known for their use in wireless communications, can also find applications in quantum communications systems. This is, for instance, relevant to satellite-based quantum communications when atmospheric turbulence and the time-varying nature of the channel can make their implementation difficult. Here, we study the application of MIMO techniques to continuous-variable (CV) quantum key distribution (QKD) in the realistic setting where a finite number of signals are exchanged. We show how data collected during the brief overpass time of low-earth-orbit satellites over ground stations can be processed to estimate MIMO channel parameters, extract a secret key, and quantify the key generation rate. Furthermore, we conjecture that the ultimate enhancement of a multiple-antenna CV-QKD system can be characterized by the product of the number of its inputs and outputs.

item.title: High-fidelity control of long-lived data qubits via a noisy mediator
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article shows that high‑fidelity gates on long‑lived storage qubits no longer demand an equally coherent mediator, because a rapid reset of the noisy auxiliary qubit can actively suppress its relaxation‑induced errors. By framing the dynamics in quantum‑trajectory language, the authors derive compact fidelity formulas that can be plugged into superconducting, trapped‑ion or spin‑based platforms, echoing recent pushes toward modular architectures where “fast” ancillae mediate interactions. Long-lived qubits are attractive for storing quantum information, but they are often difficult to control or couple directly. A common strategy is to use mediator qubits to generate effective interactions for gate implementation. However, the mediator typically has a shorter coherence time than the data qubits, so mediator relaxation and dephasing are expected to limit the achievable gate fidelity. Here, we show that this limitation can be overcome. We present a reset-assisted control method that suppresses mediator-induced errors and enables high-fidelity single- and two-qubit gates on a quantum register of long-lived data qubits. Although mediator quantum jumps render the data-qubit evolution stochastic, repeated mediator reinitialization drives the resulting evolution paths toward the desired target operation. An analytical quantum-trajectory analysis reveals the physical mechanism of error suppression and provides compact fidelity formulas for adapting the method to different platforms. Our results relax the requirement for long mediator coherence, broadening the range of mediators that can support high-fidelity control.

By exploiting the low‑filling regime—where each electron is encoded in only logarithmically many qubits—the authors demonstrate a concrete pathway to chemistry calculations on hardware that will initially have far fewer than the thousands of logical qubits traditionally assumed necessary. The results suggest that near‑term error‑corrected devices could tackle chemically relevant systems sooner, though full fault‑tolerant overheads and state‑preparation costs still need careful assessment.

Calculating molecular energies is expected to be an important application of quantum computers, but the most efficient algorithms to achieve this typically have significant space requirements. Scaling quantum processors to thousands of logical qubits is a daunting engineering challenge, so developing algorithms that run with reduced qubit requirements is of particular importance. Moreover, most algorithms are benchmarked on active spaces with about as many orbitals as electrons, missing dynamical correlation which is necessary to describe real chemistry. Capturing this correlation requires several times more orbitals than electrons, even in compact atomic-orbital basis sets. This low-filling regime favours first quantisation, where each electron is represented by a number of qubits that grows only logarithmically with the number of orbitals. Whether this approach translates into a practical advantage in orbital basis sets of realistic size, however, has been unclear. Here, we develop a first-quantised phase estimation algorithm for generic orbital basis sets, based on a non-convex sum-of-squares representation of the Hamiltonian and spectral-gap amplification. We compare it with the state-of-the-art second-quantised algorithm, compiling both with the same techniques at the logical level. For six molecules with 4 to 24 electrons in 5 to 14 times as many orbitals, our first-quantised method needs up to 16 times fewer Toffoli gates than the second-quantised algorithm in the low-qubit regime, where only a few hundred logical qubits are available. It stays cheaper up to between several hundred and about 1\,400 qubits, and its smallest qubit count is 1.4 to 2 times lower than in second quantisation. In the low-qubit and low-filling regime, our algorithm is therefore the method of choice for chemistry in orbital basis sets.

item.title: Hurst Exponent Estimation with Quantum Wavelets
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article shows how a quantum‑enhanced wavelet transform can estimate the Hurst exponent of fractional Brownian motion with root‑N statistical efficiency, a scaling that matches classical optimal estimators while exploiting quantum amplitude‑estimation primitives. By eliminating the endpoint jump through a one‑qubit mirror extension and compiling the transform from paraunitary filter banks, the authors achieve up to an order‑of‑magnitude reduction in RMSE for modest‑size data (512 points), highlighting a concrete advantage for quantum‑enabled signal‑processing and sensing tasks. The work bridges recent advances in quantum wavelet circuits with practical time‑series analysis, though its impact will depend on scaling the method to larger datasets and integrating it into near‑term hardware platforms.

How accurately can the Hurst exponent $H$ of fractional Brownian motion be estimated from repeated preparations of a single amplitude-encoded path, when every measurement interrogates the same realization? We extend the $ε$-decimated quantum nondecimated wavelet transform in three directions: we remove the endpoint jump of circular filtering, derive the sampling distribution of the estimator, and compare readouts at equal query budgets. A one-qubit mirror extension removes the jump and keeps every coefficient that straddles a fold of the same order as an interior coefficient, for any compactly supported filter and circular shift. The transform for any such filter is compiled from the paraunitary lattice of its filter bank, and the energy share of a level is the success probability of one multiply-controlled reflection, which is both the controlled unitary of a Hadamard test and the oracle of amplitude estimation. For filters with at least two vanishing moments we prove a root-$N$ central limit theorem for the log-energy contrasts, independent of the limiting path norm, so the studentized estimator is asymptotically standard normal for deterministic query budgets under which the success count at every level diverges. For sparse counts we give a working multinomial--lognormal likelihood, exact in its readout model for direct measurement, and check its coverage by simulation. For paths of length $512$, mirroring reduces RMSE by a factor of $3$--$10$ for $H\ge0.5$, and with exact shares the nondecimated db2 estimator is $6$--$14\%$ above the root Cramér--Rao bound. Hadamard level tests are less accurate than direct measurement of the leading qubits at every budget. At $H=0.9$ and $2^{20}$ queries, maximum-likelihood amplitude estimation attains RMSE $0.0347$, against $0.0451$ for direct measurement and $0.0295$ with exact shares.

item.title: Soft Mixture of Quantum Experts for Hybrid Quantum-Classical Learning
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article introduces Soft‑MoQE, a mixture‑of‑experts framework that replaces costly variational training with a classical gating network that selects and combines fixed quantum feature maps, thereby sidestepping barren‑plateau issues and dramatically lowering quantum resource demands. By achieving performance on MNIST‑derived tasks comparable to trainable quantum neural networks while using orders of magnitude less quantum optimization, it demonstrates a practical route for near‑term hybrid QML on noisy hardware. The approach builds on recent trends toward static quantum embeddings and adaptive classical routing, suggesting that smarter use of existing circuits can unlock useful quantum advantage without deep parameter tuning. Readers should note that the benchmarks rely on PCA‑reduced data, so further validation on larger, less preprocessed datasets will be needed to confirm scalability.

Quantum Machine Learning (QML) has attracted increasing interest as a possible route to construct feature representations that are difficult to reproduce with classical models. However, near-term QML architectures based on trainable parametrized quantum circuits remain affected by limited hardware resources, noise, and severe optimization difficulties such as barren plateaus. In this work we propose Soft-MoQE, a Soft Mixture of Quantum Experts architecture that replaces variational quantum training with the input-dependent selection and combination of fixed quantum feature maps. The model is composed of a heterogeneous pool of non-trainable quantum circuits, each defining a distinct embedding, and a classical gating network that learns how to weight these embeddings for each data point. We benchmark Soft-MoQE on three PCA-reduced tasks: MNIST parity, MNIST 10-class, and FashionMNIST. Soft-MoQE outperforms the single best expert, the uniform average of all experts and a linear baseline, achieving task-dependent performance comparable to that of a trainable quantum neural network, without optimizing any quantum parameter and with a quantum training cost that is lower by orders of magnitude. The analysis of the class- conditioned expert usage shows that the learned routing combines a few experts for each input, with a selection that depends on the class. These results support the learned routing among fixed quantum circuits as a trainability-aware design principle for hybrid QML.
